listeningParts.title: Joining a course for newcomers
listeningParts.contextDescription: A man who has recently moved to a new city phones a centre that runs courses for new arrivals.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Good morning, Riverside Newcomers' Centre, Joanna speaking. How can I help you?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Hello. I moved to the city about three weeks ago with my wife, for her job, and someone at the library told me you run courses and activities for people who've just arrived. Could you tell me a bit more about them?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Of course, and welcome to Riverside. We offer quite a few things, but our main service is a free orientation programme called Settling In. It helps people understand how things work here, things like registering with a doctor, opening a bank account, looking for work and using public transport. It's a series of six weekly sessions, and each one lasts two hours.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That sounds really useful. My English is fine, obviously, but there's a lot I don't understand about the local systems. The paperwork alone is confusing. When does it run?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: There are two groups. One meets on Monday mornings, from ten until twelve, and the other meets on Wednesday evenings, from half past six until half past eight, for people who work during the day.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I haven't found a job yet, so Monday mornings would suit me better.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Fine. Let me see. The next course starts on the fourth of March. Oh, sorry, I'm looking at the wrong list. The fourth is when the Wednesday group starts. The Monday group begins a week later, on the eleventh.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: The eleventh of March. Okay, that's fine.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: The sessions take place in our main building, which is at number forty-two Carver Street, in Room 3B on the second floor. There's a lift, if you need it.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: Is there anywhere to park near the building?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Not really, I'm afraid. Parking on Carver Street is very limited and quite expensive. Most people come by tram. The stop called Market Square is only a couple of minutes' walk away.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's fine. We haven't bought a car yet anyway. Is there anything I need to bring to the first session?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Just a notebook, and some form of identification, such as your passport, because we need to check it when you register. A driving licence from your home country isn't enough, unfortunately. Everything else, including the handbook, is provided.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: And is the course really free?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: The course itself is free, because it's funded by the city council. We do ask for a small contribution of two pounds a session for tea and coffee, but that's completely optional.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: That's very reasonable. My wife might want to get involved too, although she's working full-time. Do you run anything at weekends?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Yes, we have a Saturday social club, where newcomers and local volunteers meet for different activities. This month there's a walking tour of the old town, which is free, and a cooking afternoon, where people prepare a dish from their home country and share it. That one costs five pounds per person, to cover the ingredients.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: She'd love the cooking afternoon. She's a brilliant cook. Right, can I book a place on the Monday course?

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Certainly. Could I have your full name, please?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Daniel Marchetti. That's M-A-R-C-H-E-T-T-I.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Thank you. And where have you moved from, Daniel?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: From Perth, in Australia, although my father's family originally came from Italy, which explains the surname.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Lovely. And what's your address here?

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: It's Flat 7, 19 Linden Road. The postcode is RV4 8TN.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Can I also ask what kind of work you're hoping to find? Some of our sessions include talks from local employers, so it helps us to plan.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I'm a qualified nurse. I worked in a children's hospital for eight years, but I need to get my qualifications recognised here before I'm allowed to work.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: That's very common. In session four, we have a specialist adviser who helps people with exactly that, so make sure you bring copies of your certificates that week.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I will. Thank you, that's a great help.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: One last thing. How did you hear about us? We like to keep a record so we know which kind of advertising works.

dialogue.speaker: Caller
dialogue.text: I picked up a leaflet at the central library, and the librarian recommended you too.

dialogue.speaker: Adviser
dialogue.text: Wonderful. I'll send you a confirmation email this afternoon with a map and the handbook attached. We look forward to seeing you on the eleventh.

listeningParts.title: A guided visit to a migration museum
listeningParts.contextDescription: A volunteer guide introduces a group of visitors to a museum about the history of migration through a port city.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Good afternoon, everyone, and welcome to the Harbour Street Migration Museum. My name's Siobhan, and I'm one of the volunteer guides here. Before you start exploring, I'd like to give you a short introduction to the museum and explain what you'll find in each of our galleries.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: First, a little about the building. You may have noticed the old sign above the entrance. In the nineteenth century, this was the office of a shipping company, and it was here that thousands of people bought their tickets before leaving for North America and Australia. When the company closed, the building stood empty for many years, and it was almost demolished in the nineteen-nineties. A group of local residents campaigned to save it, and the museum finally opened in 2009. We chose this building precisely because so many journeys began in this very room.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: The museum tells the story of people who left this city, but also of people who arrived here, because the port has always worked in both directions. Most of our collection, around three-quarters of it, has been donated by local families. People bring us letters, photographs, suitcases and even recipes, and every object comes with a story. We're always happy to receive new donations, but please speak to a member of staff first, because we can't accept everything.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Now, the galleries. On the ground floor, just behind me, is the Departure Hall. This is where you'll find the original ticket counter, and the walls are covered with copies of the passenger lists from the ships that sailed from here. If you know that an ancestor emigrated from this port, our staff can help you search the lists. The originals are far too fragile to handle, so they're kept in our archive.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Next to it is The Crossing. Here, we've built a full-size reconstruction of the cheapest part of a nineteenth-century sailing ship, which was called steerage. You can climb into the narrow wooden bunks and get a sense of what it was like to spend six weeks or more at sea with very little light or fresh air. Some visitors find it a little uncomfortable, so you're welcome to skip it if you prefer.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Upstairs, on the first floor, is the gallery called Arrivals, which looks at the people who have come to settle in this city over the last two centuries, from many different parts of the world. I'm afraid that gallery is closed this week, because we're installing new lighting, but it should reopen on Monday.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Also on the first floor is The Kitchen Table, which is our family gallery. It's full of hands-on activities: children can dress up in historical costumes, pack a suitcase for a long journey, and taste bread made from traditional recipes. It's especially popular with school groups, so it can get quite noisy in the mornings.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: Finally, on the top floor, there's the Voices Room. This is a small, quiet space where you can sit and listen to recordings of interviews with people who've migrated, both recently and in the past. The oldest recording was made in 1962. There's also a booth where you can record your own family's story, if you'd like to. With your permission, we add these recordings to our collection, and some have been used in our exhibitions.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: A few practical points. Photography is allowed everywhere except in the Voices Room, out of respect for the people speaking. Please don't touch the objects in the glass cases, but anything with a green hand symbol beside it can be handled. And our café on the ground floor serves dishes inspired by the different communities that have settled here. Today's special, I believe, is a lentil soup from a family recipe that was donated last year.

dialogue.speaker: Guide
dialogue.text: If you have any questions, you'll find staff and volunteers in every gallery, wearing blue lanyards. The museum closes at five, but the shop stays open for another half an hour. Enjoy your visit.

listeningParts.title: An oral history project
listeningParts.contextDescription: Two sociology students, Amira and Josh, discuss their project interviewing older migrants with their tutor.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Hello, Amira, Josh. Come and sit down. So, you've finished the interviews for your oral history project. How did it go?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Really well, I think. As you know, we wanted to record the experiences of people who came to live in this town in the nineteen-sixties and seventies, before those memories are lost. In the end, we interviewed fourteen people, all aged over seventy.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: How did you find them? That can be the hardest part.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: We started by contacting community organisations, but that didn't work very well. We sent emails to about ten groups and only got two replies. What really made the difference was a lunch club for older residents at the community centre. Amira went along a few times and just chatted to people, and once they knew her, they were happy to take part, and they introduced us to their friends.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's quite typical. Trust matters much more than a formal invitation. And how did you run the interviews themselves?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: We'd prepared a list of questions, but we soon realised that following it too closely didn't work. People wanted to tell their stories in their own order, so in the end we used the questions more as a checklist and let people talk. Most interviews lasted about an hour and a half.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: And we interviewed most people in their own homes, which helped. Several of them showed us photographs or objects while they were talking, which brought back memories they might not have mentioned otherwise. One man had kept the ticket from the ship he arrived on in 1964.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Wonderful. Did anything in the interviews surprise you?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Quite a lot. We'd expected people to talk mostly about the difficulties of arriving: finding work, the weather, discrimination. And they did talk about those things. But what came up again and again was food. Nearly everyone described how hard it was at first to find the ingredients they were used to, and how important cooking was in keeping a connection with home.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: The other surprise for me was how many of them had planned to stay only a few years. Almost half said they'd intended to earn some money and then go back, but then they had children, and their children grew up here, and somehow they never left.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's a very common pattern in migration research. It's sometimes called the myth of return. Now, I'd like to talk about the problems of using memory as evidence. How reliable do you think your interviewees' memories were?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: That's something we discussed a lot. Some of the dates people gave were clearly wrong. One woman said she arrived in 1968, but later she mentioned an event that happened in 1971 as if it was just after she came. So we checked dates against other sources where we could.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. But remember that the value of oral history isn't mainly in the precise facts. It's in how people understood and felt about their experiences. A wrong date doesn't make the story worthless.

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: That's what we've been arguing in our draft. We're treating the interviews as evidence of how people remember and give meaning to their lives, rather than as a record of exactly what happened.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Exactly. Now, what about the practical side? You've transcribed everything?

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: Almost. Transcription took far longer than we expected. Each hour of recording took us about six hours to type up, partly because some people switched between English and their first language.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: That's normal, I'm afraid. And you got signed consent forms from everyone?

dialogue.speaker: Josh
dialogue.text: Yes, from all fourteen. Two people asked us not to use their real names, so we've given them different names in the report. And three people asked to see the transcripts before we use any quotations, so we're posting those to them this week.

dialogue.speaker: Tutor
dialogue.text: Good. One more suggestion: the town museum is collecting recordings like these for its archive. If your interviewees agree, you could offer them the recordings. That way, your work will be useful long after the project is marked.

dialogue.speaker: Amira
dialogue.text: We'd love that. We'll ask them when we send the transcripts.

listeningParts.title: The demographic transition
listeningParts.contextDescription: A lecture in a population geography course on how and why population growth changes as countries develop.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Good morning, everyone. Today we're going to look at one of the most influential ideas in population studies, the demographic transition model. It attempts to explain how the population of a country changes as it moves from a traditional society to a modern, industrial one. The basic idea was first set out by the American demographer Warren Thompson in 1929, and it was developed further in the nineteen-forties by Frank Notestein and others.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: The model is usually described in four stages. In the first stage, both birth rates and death rates are high. This is typical of an agricultural society before modern medicine. Many children are born, but many also die young, from disease, poor diet and periods of famine. Because births and deaths roughly balance each other, the population grows very slowly, if at all. For most of human history, this was the normal situation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the second stage, the death rate begins to fall. This happens because of improvements in the food supply, in sanitation, particularly clean water and proper sewers, and later in medicine, such as vaccination. But the birth rate stays high, because people's attitudes and habits about family size don't change overnight. The result is a period of very rapid population growth. In England, for example, this happened during the nineteenth century, when the population grew several times over.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the third stage, the birth rate also starts to fall. Demographers have identified several reasons for this. As people move from farms to cities, children are no longer needed to work on the land, and instead become an economic cost, because they have to be fed, housed and educated for many years. As more children survive, parents no longer need to have many children to make sure that some reach adulthood. And perhaps most importantly, as girls and women receive more education and enter paid work, they tend to marry later and have fewer children. Access to contraception also plays a role.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: In the fourth stage, both birth and death rates are low, and the population is fairly stable again, but at a much higher level than before. An important figure here is what's called replacement level fertility, which is about two point one children per woman in countries with low death rates. That's the number needed for each generation to replace itself.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: One thing that surprises students is that a population can keep growing for decades after fertility has fallen to replacement level. This is known as population momentum. It happens because, after a period of high birth rates, there are very large numbers of young people who are just reaching the age when they start their own families. Even if each couple has only two children, the total number of births stays high for a generation.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: Some geographers have added a fifth stage, in which the birth rate falls below the death rate and the population starts to shrink. Japan is the clearest example. Its population has been falling since around 2010, and a growing proportion of its people are over sixty-five, which creates serious challenges for healthcare, pensions and the labour market.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: So, how useful is the model? It certainly describes the history of many countries quite well, but it has been criticised in several ways. First, it was based on European experience, and it assumes that other countries will follow the same path, which isn't necessarily true. Second, the speed of change has varied enormously. In parts of East Asia, the transition happened much more quickly than in Europe. In South Korea, for instance, the average woman had around six children in 1960, but by the mid nineteen-eighties, fertility had fallen below replacement level. Today, South Korea has one of the lowest fertility rates in the world.

dialogue.speaker: Lecturer
dialogue.text: And third, and this leads into next week's topic, the model largely ignores migration. In many countries today, immigration has become the main source of population growth, and in some regions emigration has been the main cause of decline. We'll look at that next week.

readingPassages.title: Ellis Island: gateway to America
paragraphs: For more than sixty years, a small island in New York Harbor was the first piece of American soil that millions of immigrants ever stood on. Between 1892 and 1954, around twelve million people passed through the immigration station on Ellis Island, within sight of the Statue of Liberty. For most of them, the experience lasted only a few hours, but it became one of the defining moments of their lives, and the island has since become a powerful symbol of the United States as a nation of immigrants.

Before Ellis Island opened, immigration to New York was managed not by the national government but by New York State, which ran a reception centre called Castle Garden at the southern tip of Manhattan. By the late 1880s, the system was struggling to cope with the growing number of arrivals, and there were frequent complaints of corruption, with newcomers being cheated by dishonest money changers and agents. In 1890, the federal government took control of immigration and chose Ellis Island as the site of a new station. The island was so small that it had to be enlarged with landfill to several times its original size.

The station opened on 1 January 1892. The first immigrant to be registered was Annie Moore, a teenage girl from County Cork in Ireland, who had travelled with her two younger brothers to join their parents in New York. However, the original wooden buildings did not last long. In June 1897, a fire destroyed them, along with many immigration records dating back several decades. They were replaced by a fireproof building of brick and limestone, which opened in December 1900 and still stands today.

Not every passenger had to visit the island. First- and second-class passengers were usually inspected briefly on board their ship and allowed to go straight ashore, on the assumption that people who could afford expensive tickets were unlikely to become a burden on the state. It was the much larger number of third-class, or steerage, passengers who were taken by ferry to Ellis Island. The volume of traffic was enormous. In 1907, the busiest year in the station's history, more than a million immigrants arrived, and on one day in April of that year, over eleven thousand people were processed.

The inspection began before most immigrants realised it. As they climbed the stairs to the vast Registry Room, doctors watched them carefully, looking for signs of illness or disability. Anyone who seemed unwell had a letter marked on their clothing in chalk: 'H' for suspected heart problems, for example, or 'E' for the eyes. One of the most feared tests was the examination for trachoma, a contagious eye disease, in which doctors turned back the eyelids using a small hook. Those who were marked were taken aside for a more detailed examination, and some were sent to the island's hospital.

Next came the legal inspection. An inspector, often assisted by an interpreter, asked each immigrant around thirty questions, including their name, occupation, destination and how much money they had. The answers were checked against the ship's manifest, the passenger list that had been drawn up at the port of departure. A popular story claims that officials frequently changed immigrants' surnames at this stage, giving them simpler, more 'American' names. Historians have found no evidence for this. Inspectors worked from the lists prepared in Europe, and name changes usually happened later, when immigrants or their children chose to adapt their names themselves.

For the great majority, the process ended well. Only about two per cent of those who arrived were refused entry, most commonly because of serious contagious disease or because officials believed they would be unable to support themselves. Nevertheless, for families separated by such decisions, the island earned a painful nickname: the 'Island of Tears'. From the 1920s, however, its role changed. New laws, especially the Immigration Act of 1924, introduced strict quotas that sharply reduced immigration, particularly from southern and eastern Europe. Inspections were increasingly carried out at American consulates abroad, and Ellis Island was used mainly for detention and deportation until it closed in November 1954.

For many years after its closure, the buildings were abandoned and fell into ruin. In 1965, the island was made part of the Statue of Liberty National Monument, and after a major restoration, the main building reopened as a museum of immigration in 1990. Today, it attracts millions of visitors, many of whom come to search for their own ancestors in the passenger records. It is often estimated that around four in ten Americans have at least one ancestor who entered the country through Ellis Island.

readingPassages.title: Why people move
paragraphs: According to the United Nations, around 281 million people were living outside their country of birth in 2020, roughly 3.6 per cent of the world's population. The figure has risen steadily for decades, and migration is rarely out of the news. Yet it is worth remembering that the vast majority of people never move abroad at all, and that far more people move within their own countries, usually from the countryside to cities, than across international borders. Explaining why some people move while most stay where they are has occupied geographers for well over a century.

One of the first serious attempts was made by Ernst Georg Ravenstein, a German-born geographer working in London, who studied British census data and published his 'laws of migration' in 1885. Ravenstein observed that most migrants travelled only short distances, and that migration often happened in steps, with people moving from villages to small towns and later to large cities. He noted that each flow of migrants tended to produce a smaller counter-flow in the opposite direction, and that large towns grew more through migration than through births. Many of his observations still hold remarkably well today.

In 1966, the American sociologist Everett Lee proposed a more general framework. Migration, he argued, is influenced by factors at the place of origin, such as unemployment or conflict, which 'push' people away, and by factors at the destination, such as jobs or safety, which 'pull' them towards it. Crucially, Lee added that between the two lie 'intervening obstacles', including distance, cost and immigration laws, and that personal circumstances, such as age, family ties and attitudes to risk, determine how each individual responds. The same conditions might drive one person to leave while another stays.

Economists have traditionally explained migration as the result of individual decisions: people move when the wages they expect to earn elsewhere outweigh the costs of moving. In the 1980s, however, economists such as Oded Stark proposed what became known as the new economics of labour migration. In this view, migration is often a decision taken by a household rather than an individual. A family in a rural area, for example, may send one member to work in a city or abroad, not only to increase its income, but to reduce risk. If the harvest fails, the money sent home will help the family to survive.

That money, known as remittances, has become one of the most important financial flows in the world. The World Bank estimates that migrants sent more than six hundred billion dollars to low- and middle-income countries in 2023, considerably more than these countries received in official development aid. In some smaller economies, remittances are equivalent to a fifth or more of national income. Sending money is still expensive, however, with fees averaging around six per cent of the amount sent, and one of the United Nations' Sustainable Development Goals is to reduce this to below three per cent.

A less obvious finding is that the poorest people rarely migrate internationally. Moving abroad requires money for travel, documents and the period before finding work, as well as education and contacts. As a result, when poor countries begin to develop, emigration often increases rather than falls, at least for a time, because more people can afford to leave. Only when incomes reach a much higher level does emigration usually decline. This pattern, sometimes called the 'migration hump', suggests that development aid is unlikely to reduce migration in the short term, despite what some politicians claim.

Once a migration flow has begun, it often continues because of social networks. Migrants who have settled in a new country can provide information, accommodation and help in finding work to relatives and friends who follow them, reducing both the cost and the risk of moving. This process, known as chain migration, helps to explain why migrants from a particular village or region are often concentrated in particular cities or even particular streets abroad, and why migration flows can continue long after the original economic reasons have disappeared.

Increasingly, researchers are also asking how climate change will affect migration. Droughts, floods and rising sea levels can destroy livelihoods, and a 2021 World Bank report projected that, without strong action, up to 216 million people could be forced to move within their own countries by 2050 because of climate-related pressures. Most experts stress, however, that environmental change rarely acts alone. It interacts with poverty, conflict and government policy, and most people affected by disasters move only short distances, often temporarily. Ravenstein, it seems, would not have been surprised.

readingPassages.title: Between two worlds
paragraphs: For most people, the question 'Where are you from?' has a simple answer. For millions of migrants and their children, it does not. Someone born in Marseille to Algerian parents, or raised in Toronto by a Filipino mother and an Irish father, may feel that a single answer would be incomplete, or even untrue. How people come to understand who they are when they belong to more than one culture is one of the central questions in the study of migration, and the answers researchers have given have changed considerably over the past century.

For much of the twentieth century, the dominant assumption, particularly in the United States, was that immigrants would gradually assimilate. The popular image was the 'melting pot', a phrase made famous by Israel Zangwill's play of that name, first performed in 1908, in which people of different origins were imagined dissolving into a new, shared national identity. On this view, the loss of a heritage language and customs over two or three generations was not only inevitable but desirable, a sign of successful adjustment to a new home.

From the 1970s onwards, the Canadian psychologist John Berry offered a more complex picture. He suggested that people living between cultures face two separate questions: to what extent do they wish to maintain their heritage culture, and to what extent do they wish to take part in the wider society? The combination of answers produces four strategies. Assimilation means giving up one's original culture for the new one; separation means holding on to the original culture while avoiding contact with the wider society; integration means maintaining both; and marginalisation describes people who have lost their connection with their original culture without finding a place in the new one.

Much research has supported the value of integration. A large international study led by Berry and his colleagues, published in 2006, examined more than five thousand immigrant adolescents in thirteen countries. Young people who were involved in both their heritage culture and the national culture generally showed the best psychological well-being and adjusted best at school, while those with no clear attachment to either did worst. Berry himself stressed, however, that integration can only be chosen freely when the receiving society is open to cultural diversity. In my view, this point is too often forgotten: migrants cannot integrate into a society that refuses to accept them.

Language is often where the tension is felt most sharply. The sociolinguist Joshua Fishman, who spent much of his career studying minority languages, described a pattern that has been observed in many immigrant communities in the United States: the first generation speaks the heritage language, the second generation understands it but often prefers English, and by the third generation it has largely been lost. Many grandparents and grandchildren today cannot hold a real conversation. I believe this loss is rarely chosen deliberately; it happens quietly, through the pressures of school, friendship and work.

Some people grow up not between two cultures but among several. In the 1950s, the American sociologist Ruth Hill Useem, who had lived in India with her family, introduced the term 'third culture kids' to describe children who spend a significant part of their childhood outside their parents' home culture. Such children often develop a 'third culture' made up of elements of both, and frequently say that they feel at home everywhere and nowhere. Many adapt easily to new places, but some describe a lasting sense of restlessness and difficulty answering the simple question of where home is.

Theorists of identity have pushed the argument further. The cultural theorist Stuart Hall argued in 1990 that cultural identity is a matter of 'becoming' as well as 'being': something that is constantly produced and transformed, rather than a fixed essence inherited from the past. Even national identities, the political scientist Benedict Anderson famously suggested, are 'imagined communities', since the members of a nation will never meet most of their fellow members, yet feel connected to them. If identities are constructed rather than given, then there is nothing unnatural about building one from more than one source.

None of this means that mixed identities are always comfortable. Second-generation migrants frequently report being seen as foreign in the country of their birth and as foreign again when they visit their parents' homeland. Yet I would argue that the problem lies less in the individuals themselves than in other people's expectations that identity should be single and simple. A person who is both Algerian and French is not half of each, but wholly both. In my view, the sooner societies accept this, the easier it will be for millions of people to answer the question 'Where are you from?' honestly.
